name: Winch size
seoTitle: Winch size Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Winch size: work out ground type from the damaged wheels and the pull. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the damaged wheels, the pull and the centre of gravity and the Winch size calculator solves for ground type. That makes it useful for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Winch size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Winch size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports ground type in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the mode and the vehicle type); then you type in the damaged wheels, the pull, the centre of gravity and the pull (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Winch size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Ground type=weight ÷ rolling resistance
Damage resistance=damaged wheels × weight ÷ original wheels
Original wheels=damaged wheels × weight ÷ damage resistance
Damage resistance=-direction × gradient resistance 2 + pull − rolling resistance
Height=centre of gravity × weight ÷ pull
Degree of slope=gradient resistance 2 ÷ weight

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — I want to set to right a rolled over load, Mode set to Choose vehicle type, Vehicle type set to Small car and Ground type set to Road — it reports Weight = 1000 kg.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Weight = 1000 kg should be roughly the size you expected from I want to set to right a rolled over load and Mode set to Choose vehicle type.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Winch size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the damaged wheels, the pull and the centre of gravity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Winch size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns ground type, derived from the damaged wheels, the pull and the centre of gravity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Winch size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the damaged wheels, the pull and the centre of gravity, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Weight = 1000 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Winch size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
